I rang in the new year of 2000 at work with my IT coworkers. We had spent years preparing and updating our systems that showed any signs of potential Y2K issues or other things that could go wrong due to the date change. I was a programmer working for a large corporation that had me embedded in a chemical plant developing various software systems for all aspects of the business. I was responsible for managing the testing and remediation for all in-house developed desktop and intranet based systems for the Y2K project. I spent two years working with my software development team to make sure anything that was remotely critical to the operations of the plant was fixed, patched or replaced if there were suspected issues. All of our in-house stuff tested well but some things got patched or replaced since we had the budget to do it. The company had partnered with a similar plant in New Zealand which would the first industrialized country to experience the date change. Since they had similar systems and we had shared so much with them over those two years, we knew early in the day that we were likely safe and that nothing significant in NZ blew up or failed. We still had to stay for the date change in our time zone so we stocked up with all kinds of party food and non-alcoholic drinks (boo!) to have some fun while we waited. Once midnight rolled around and we ran all of our test cases, nothing failed and we were still very much alive and the news was not reporting any incidents. We made it through because we planned and worked hard to have the big "scare" be a nothing burger, but hey, if the public wants to think it was all hype and no danger, well then all I can say is "on behalf of all the programmers, database developers, network engineers and the whole range of IT professionals who worked hard to make it a non-event, you're welcome".
